"If quails were banished from the tables of the ancients, as Pliny asserts, because they suffer from epilepsy, then oxen, goats, rams and capons too will have to be banished, since all these animals have also been observed to suffer from the same disease." Aldrovandi, loc. cit.
Compare v. 52 of the same Ps. LXXVIII.

I. E. Faber, on Harmar II, p. 445, holds the same view, without adequate reason.

"The noun קדים seems rather to be said generally of wind, and of a more violent wind, as in Psal. XLVIII, 8. For there is a kind of parallelism, not indeed noted by Lowth, On the Sacred Poetry of the Hebrews, lecture 19, yet not very infrequent, in which something is first said universally and generally, and then designated more specifically, as in v. 43: when he performed his miracles in Egypt, and his wonders in the region of Tanis. And the Syriac translator too seems to have understood the passage thus, rendering: ܐܫܒ ܪܘܚܐ ܒܫܡܝܐ, he stirred up the winds in the heaven, unless you prefer to pronounce ܪܘܚܐ as wind." Thus Schnurrer, loc. cit.
Rather, from Arabia Felix or Yemen, as Oedmann rightly observes, Fasc. 4, p. 65, where the opinions of others are also assessed.

That is, at the time when, leaving Europe at the beginning of autumn, they make for southern lands; the matter itself shows that a south wind is contrary to them. Nor are the words of Aristotle, book 8, ch. 12, quoted above, to be understood otherwise; Pliny wrongly interpreted them to mean that quails never fly when the south wind blows, and for this he is also criticized by our author in what immediately follows. Aldrovandi, Ornithol. II, p. 156, therefore rightly, after quoting the words of Belon which Bochart himself presently cites, continues thus: "For if in flying they use the north wind, and refrain from flight in a south wind, as we have said from Pliny and Aristotle, it must be declared that they fly with a contrary wind when they come to us; which plainly appears to conflict with reason and with our senses. For the north wind, which takes its name [aquilo] from the very swift flight of the eagle [aquila], is a very fast wind and also very violent; quails, by contrast, have a very weak flight because of the excessive heaviness of their body. How, then, they could come to us while this wind blows, I cannot at all persuade myself, nor would anyone else easily persuade me. Therefore I think that when leaving us they use the help of the wind, but by no means when coming to us; indeed, unless a north wind is granted for their departure, they reach the desired places with difficulty." Buffon holds the same opinion on those words of Aristotle, Hist. Nat. des Oiseaux vol. 2, p. 461: I believe indeed that it is the wind that helps quails make their journey, not the north wind but a favourable wind; just as it is not the south wind that delays their course but a contrary wind; and this is true in all countries where these birds have a considerable crossing to make over the seas. The Commander Godeheu has very well remarked that in spring quails land on Malta only with the north-west wind, which is contrary to them for reaching Provence, and that on their return it is the south-east wind that brings them to this island, [II, 667] because with that wind they cannot land in Barbary: we even see that the Author of Nature used this means, as the most consistent with the general laws he had established, to send numerous flocks of quails to the Israelites in the desert.
That is, חמר, which is in the text, where it is the name of a measure, is the same as כר. See Ezech. XLV, 11. 14. Esr. VII, 22.

But then, I should think, חמרים חמרים would have been added. You will say it is incredible that the quails over that whole space (of a day's journey around the camp (v. 31)) were heaped up so that everywhere they stood two cubits high. But the one who wrote this book about the wanderings of the Israelites through the Arabian desert, the fourth of those that bear Moses' name, meant to relate incredible things. That it was by no means written by Moses, however, we shall prove at another time.
